sections.h2: Ways to sell quickly in Moline
sections.html:
Moline owners have three choices: an agent, a buyer found without one, or a purchaser who pays cash and takes the house as found. That last choice closes soonest, with an offer shaped by the work needed.

Moline is a Quad Cities city, and the buyers who show up here are shaped by that. Some are workers tied to the large employers along the river, some are investors, and some are families moving within the Illinois and Iowa sides of the metro. Knowing which group your house suits helps you choose the route.

What follows is local: housing figures, neighborhoods and school boundaries, the city's building office, and the filing rules at the Rock Island County Recorder.

Moline counted 42,985 people in 2020 and an estimated 42,362 in July 2025, a dip of 1.4 percent. The median owned home is valued at $146,300 and median rent is $900 (2020 to 2024). Owners live in 67.3 percent of homes, across 18,289 households of about 2.29 people. Household income at the median is $67,701, and the average drive to work is just 18.0 minutes.

  • At these prices a repair bill takes a larger bite of the sale price, so get quotes before you decide to renovate.
  • A short commute and a large employment base make renting out a house a realistic option for some owners, and buyers who rent houses out may bid on yours.
  • The estimate has slipped a little since 2020, so buyers can be choosy, and a house needing work may wait longer on the open market.

Moline sits on a bluff between the Mississippi and Rock rivers, and deep ravines cut the high ground into natural neighborhoods. Neighborhood associations work with the city, and the downtown area is known as Moline Centre. Other neighborhood names in common use include Floreciente, Olde Towne, Uptown, Overlook, Wharton, Hamilton Heights, Prospect Park, Park Hill, Forest Hill and Highland. A listing that names the neighborhood reads more clearly to local buyers than a street address alone.

Moline School District No. 40 covers most of the city, with about 7,500 students in twelve elementary schools, two middle schools named for John Deere and Woodrow Wilson, and Moline High School. Pieces of the city on the east side belong to East Moline District 37 and United Township High School District 30, and a southwest piece belongs to Rock Island-Milan District 41. Verify the district for an address before you advertise one.

Interstate 74 runs straight through the city and splits it into two roughly equal halves, and Interstate 280 circles the Quad Cities. Moline is about 165 miles west of Chicago.

Deere and Company keeps its corporate headquarters in Moline, and Kone's U.S. division is based in the city as well. Black Hawk College and the Quad Cities campus of Western Illinois University are both in Moline, and Quad Cities International Airport sits on the south edge of town. South Park Mall and a string of big-box centers make the city a retail hub.

The downtown arena, Vibrant Arena at The MARK, and John Deere Commons draw events that fill nearby restaurants and hotels. Houses within a short drive of these destinations tend to be pitched to commuters and renters, so say so in your listing.

sections.h2: Winter wear and what buyers inspect
sections.html:
Moline sees 43 days a year when the high never climbs above freezing and 31.6 inches of snow a season, and summers run hot and humid. Buyers will check the roof, the furnace and the air conditioner, because a house here works both systems hard. The freeze-thaw cycle also tests sidewalks, driveways and foundation walls.

Houses on bluffs and ravine edges also deserve a look at drainage and grading. If a lot slopes toward the foundation, expect an inspector to flag it.

The Building and Inspections Division is at the City Services Center, 1830 6th Avenue, and visitors use the north entrance on 6th Avenue. It handles building permits and plan reviews, building inspections, contractor registration, food establishment licensing and code enforcement.

Code complaints about housing, nuisance, vegetation, zoning and signs go through the City's Neighborhood Improvement Officer, who also works with the neighborhood groups. If your house has an open complaint or a citation, resolve it or ask the city what a closing needs, because a title company can discover it.

  • Pull permit records for any remodel, deck, roof or mechanical work done in your years of ownership.
  • Ask the division how to close out any permit that was opened but never finished.
  • Ask the water and sewer divisions about final billing before the closing date.

The city publishes its Code of Ordinances online for anyone who wants to check a rule before listing.

sections.h2: How a Moline deed gets recorded
sections.html:
Recording for a Moline address takes place in neighboring Rock Island, at the Recorder's second-floor office at 1504 3rd Avenue (309-558-3360). Counter hours are weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The county lays out format rules: white letter-size paper, a clear 3 by 5 inch box at the top right of page one, no staples or tape, black ink and type of at least 10 points. The document must name its preparer and a return address, and a deed adds the grantee's address and a spot for the tax bill mailing address.

Under 35 ILCS 200/31-15 the state charges fifty cents for every $500 of value. Call the Recorder to ask whether a county or city stamp is added.

sections.h2: What a Moline seller should have ready before an offer
sections.html:
Start with the disclosure report. State law, 765 ILCS 77/20, has the seller complete each item and hand the report over ahead of the signed contract.

Then pull together the closing file: parcel number, newest tax bill, any loan payoff figure and the permit history. A rented house also needs its leases and tenant contacts, which a buyer will want to read.

Weigh at least two offers by what you would net, not by the headline figure. Ask each buyer who covers transfer stamps, which repairs they expect and how fast they can close.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and loan approval, which is why a cash sale tends to close soonest. The deed still has to meet the county's format rules, so check the checklist above before you sign.

faqs.q: Do houses sell quickly in Moline?
faqs.a: It varies. The median home value of $146,300 is modest, and the population estimate has eased since 2020, so a house needing repairs may linger on the market. A purchase by a cash buyer is usually the quickest way out.

faqs.q: Which office files a Moline deed?
faqs.a: The Rock Island County Recorder, whose second-floor counter at 1504 3rd Avenue opens weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call 309-558-3360.

faqs.q: What formatting does Rock Island County insist on for deeds?
faqs.a: Letter-size white paper, an empty 3 by 5 inch area in the upper right of page one, black ink at 10 points or larger, nothing attached, and lines naming the preparer and where to send the document back. Deeds also carry the grantee's address and the address for tax bills.

faqs.q: Who approves building work on a Moline house?
faqs.a: The city's Building and Inspections Division reviews plans, issues permits, runs inspections and registers contractors. Contact it at the City Services Center on 6th Avenue before starting a project.

faqs.q: What paperwork must a Moline seller give the buyer?
faqs.a: A finished residential disclosure report, in the buyer's hands before the contract is signed (765 ILCS 77/20). The state transfer tax, fifty cents per $500, is paid when the deed is recorded.
